questions.learningObjective: Explain how the frequency of a standing wave scales with mode number
questions.stem: Card 1: our string fixed at both ends shows three half-wavelengths across its length. What would the standing wave look like with six?

options.text: The same string would carry a standing wave with six half-wavelengths, at twice the frequency.
The same string would carry a standing wave with six half-wavelengths, at six times the frequency.
options.misconception: believes the frequency scales with the number of segments

options.text: The standing wave would keep three half-wavelengths but with nodes twice as far apart.
options.misconception: believes the pattern spacing changes rather than the pattern

options.text: The standing wave would not fit at all, since the string length is already used up.
options.misconception: believes a higher mode needs a longer string

questions.explanation: For a string fixed at both ends the allowed wavelengths are 2L/n, so n half-wavelengths means n times the fundamental frequency. Six half-wavelengths is twice the frequency of three, on the same string.

options.misconception: believes amplitude survives the change of medium

questions.explanation: The source sets the frequency, and it is fixed whatever the medium does to the speed. Entering water slows the sound, which shortens the wavelength, so speed and wavelength change while frequency holds.

options.misconception: believes heavier materials must always slow waves

options.text: Rubber is the fastest, because rubber is elastic and stores the most energy.

The table is unusable, since the wave speed of a solid does not depend on its material.
options.misconception: believes wave speed is the same in all solids

questions.explanation: Steel at 340 m/s is fastest and rubber at 60 m/s slowest. String speed follows the square root of tension over mass per unit length, so a light material for its strength carries the wave quicker.
